items.prompt: What are the two things every review comment carries?

A technical fact and a social signal
A score and a short summary

items.prompt: Reviewer A's 'This is wrong, use a hashmap' got which part right?
items.explanation: The bug was real; the delivery told the author they had done something wrong.

items.prompt: A comment can be technically correct and still cost a lot. True or false?
choices: False, correct comments are always cheap
False, only wrong comments cost anything
items.explanation: Correctness of the fact says nothing about the cost of the signal.

items.prompt: 'You did this wrong' is mostly a statement about...
items.explanation: The subject is a person, so it reads as a verdict on them.

items.prompt: The social signal in a comment answers which question for the author?
choices: Which file should I open next?
How does this reviewer see me?
How long will the CI run take?
items.explanation: Authors read the signal as part of the message, whether or not it was intended.

items.prompt: What does the author have to handle before fixing when the signal is bad?
choices: A brand new build system setup
items.explanation: Feeling judged adds work before the technical step can begin.

items.prompt: Which is the 'fact' in 'This lookup goes quadratic, you should know better'?
items.explanation: The first clause is checkable about the code; the second is about the person.

items.prompt: Why is the unit's subject fact versus signal and not bug-finding skill?
choices: Reviewer A failed to find the bug
Reviewer B found a different bug
Both reviewers found it equally well
items.explanation: The bug and skill were identical; only delivery differed.

items.prompt: Two reviewers report the same missing input check. One writes 'Sloppy, you never validate input.' The other writes 'This endpoint accepts negative quantities; should we reject them?' What differs?
choices: Nothing; both comments are received identically
Only the technical fact each comment reports
Only the number of words each comment uses
The signal sent about the author, not the fact reported
items.explanation: Both name the same defect; the first also passes a verdict on the person.
items.reference:
Fact and signal
🔧 fact: what is wrong with the code
🤝 signal: how the reviewer sees the author
⚠️ wrong signal makes a correct review costly
Why: every comment states a fact and sends a signal, and a right fact can still be delivered at a high cost.
items.learnMore:
A comment is two messages

The fact is what you would put in a bug report. The signal is what the author infers about how you regard them. Both arrive together, and the author cannot read one without the other.

Common mistake

Assuming a technically correct comment is automatically a good comment.
items.reflection: Think of a teacher returning an essay with only the word 'wrong' across it versus a note pointing at one paragraph. What did each tell the student beyond the correction itself?

items.prompt: A comment is correct in every technical detail yet the author goes silent for days. Which diagnosis fits best?

The author is simply slow at making fixes
The signal was costly even though the fact was right
items.explanation: Correct facts can still carry a signal that makes acting on them expensive.

items.prompt: A review costs the author a day of back-and-forth about what 'cleanup needed' meant, then ten minutes to fix. What was the main cost?

items.reference:
Where the cost lands
⏳ delay while managing a feeling
🔁 extra round-trip for a vague comment

items.learnMore:
The bug is cheap, the overhead isn't

Fixing the lookup takes minutes. Three days were spent on defending, clarifying and guessing priorities. Good framing removes that overhead rather than being polite for its own sake.

Common mistake

Treating framing as manners instead of as a way to cut avoidable work.

Why async review is harder

💬 PR comment: words only
⏱️ replies take hours

No tone in text

Face-to-face, a smile or a pause softens or clarifies a sentence. In a thread, the words are all that survives, read later and out of context.

Common mistake

Assuming the author will read your comment in the tone you meant it.

items.prompt: Which is code-directed?

items.prompt: Which comment aims at the code and not the person?
choices: 'The retry loop never stops if the server keeps failing'
'You wrote a retry loop that never stops when the server fails'
'Whoever wrote this loop forgot to add any kind of limit'
'Your loop is broken again, as it was in the last two PRs'
items.explanation: Only the first makes the loop the subject without naming a person.
items.reference:
Person versus code subject
👤 'you did this wrong' → defend
📄 'this goes quadratic' → check
🎯 same defect, different subject
Why: making the code the subject removes the need to judge whether you are being judged.
items.learnMore:
Change the subject, keep the fact

'You forgot X' puts the author on trial. 'X isn't handled here' puts the code on the table. The report is identical and the reaction is not.

Common mistake

Believing code-directed wording is only softer tone, rather than less overhead.

items.prompt: A reviewer asks 'Could this use the existing helper?' The author replies the helper is deprecated. What did the framing allow?

Statement versus question

Turning every comment into a hedge, or asking a question when you mean a requirement.

items.explanation: It must be fixed before merge.

items.prompt: The technique aims to remove...

items.prompt: A reviewer sees a hard-coded API key in a diff. Best comment?
choices: 'Worth considering moving this to an environment variable at some point down the line?'
'`blocking:` this commits a live API key. Remove it and rotate the key before merge.'
'Maybe move this somewhere else when you have a free moment, no rush at all?'
'Hmm, is it really safe to leave a key like this in the file? Maybe we could look at it later?'
items.explanation: It is specific, aimed at the code, and clearly mandatory.
items.reference:
When softening is wrong
🔐 security / data loss
🚧 use `blocking:` and a statement
❌ 'worth considering?' reads as optional
Why: framing exists to remove unnecessary friction, not to make mandatory fixes look optional.
items.learnMore:
Match framing to severity

Debatable choices suit questions. Defects that are not matters of opinion need a plain statement and a `blocking:` label.

Common mistake

Applying the question rewrite mechanically to a defect.

items.explanation: Real-time exchange.

items.prompt: Does escalating mean the framing failed?

items.prompt: 'No new information' means...

items.prompt: Round one: reviewer states a concern. Round two: author restates the original choice with the same reasons. Reviewer restates the concern. Next move?
choices: Write a more careful third comment
Close the PR and reopen later
Move to a call or pairing
items.explanation: Two rounds with no new information triggers escalation.
items.reference:
Escalating a stuck thread
🔁 two rounds, no new information
📞 move to a call or pairing
🧱 wording can't fix a medium problem
Why: when two rounds add no new information, the medium is the obstacle, so leave the text.
items.learnMore:
Know the signal

One disagreement is normal. Two rounds of restated positions mean both understand and still differ. A short call resolves it faster than another comment.

Common mistake

Rewriting the same point a third time in text.
